body.text: India has called for greater cooperation with countries of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) grouping to bring stability to Asia amid mounting uncertainties of conflict, protectionism, and competition among nations, besides realignment in a fragmenting post-World War II order.

Speaking at the 23rd India-ASEAN Summit in Manila on November 17, Prime Minister Narendra Modi underlined India’s unwavering support for ASEAN’s unity and centrality in the region and in Asia at large.

“India and ASEAN represent nearly one-fourth of the world’s population. That is why it is essential to ensure that our future is shaped not by competition, but by cooperation. We have both the capabilities and the shared resolve to achieve this. Together, we can make this region a symbol of peace and stability,” Modi said in his opening remarks at the India-ASEAN Summit. “We firmly believe that India’s growth and ASEAN’s prosperity are deeply interconnected,” he added.

Digital technology, defense, and space have been the new areas of collaboration for India and ASEAN in recent years. ASEAN is one of India’s top trading partners with annual commerce worth about $122 billion.

Briefing reporters in Manila after the India-ASEAN summit, Rudrendra Tandon, Secretary East in India’s External Affairs Ministry, said that Modi had told his ASEAN counterparts at a closed-door session that the two sides “must work together to become drivers of stability in Asia,” given the current geopolitical flux that has thrown up common challenges for India and ASEAN.

To speed up the momentum of cooperation, Modi suggested that India and ASEAN focus on the maritime domain, as they are maritime neighbors. Increasing maritime connectivity and security, boosting scientific research and disaster management, and encouraging greater coordination between port authorities and the coast guards of India and ASEAN countries were some of the practical ways Modi recommended to cement this cooperation, Tandon added.

Cybercrime and fraud prevention, creation of reliable supply chains, critical minerals, space collaboration for agriculture and resource management, and pooling of expertise to promote nuclear energy were the other proposals Modi put forward for deepening India and ASEAN cooperation. Modi also announced an e-visa facility for tourists from ASEAN countries to strengthen ties among the people of India and ASEAN.

To ensure better coordination on disaster management, especially earthquakes, cyclones, and tsunamis, India and ASEAN agreed to strengthen regular consultations on early warning systems through sharing of satellite data, seismic monitoring information, and meteorological forecasts, a joint statement said. The two sides would also use space-based data for disaster risk assessment, monitoring, and forecasting.

Besides the India-ASEAN Summit, Modi also attended the 21st East Asia Summit that brings together 11 members of ASEAN and its six dialogue partners. Besides India, the other dialogue partners include Australia, China, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, Russia, and the United States.

In his speech, Modi pointed out that ongoing conflicts were increasing pressure on food, fuel, and fertilizer supplies. “Ships and seafarers are also being targeted on international waterways,” he said, adding: “Today, what the world needs most is peace, stability, and predictability.” Tandon said that Modi had proposed a “Seafarers’ Safety Initiative” to strengthen emergency response.

India’s proposal comes against the backdrop of Indian seafarers being killed due to the Russia-Ukraine and Iran-U.S. conflicts. At least 15 Indian seafarers have been killed in the Iran-U.S. conflict, while five more have died in attacks in the Black Sea. India is reported to have more than 320,000 seafarers – the second highest in the world after the Philippines – and more than 18,000 are on vessels in West Asia.
At the East Asia Summit, Modi also expressed India’s commitment to a “free, open, inclusive, and rules-based Indo-Pacific region.”

India’s current engagement with ASEAN and the East Asia Summit comes at a critical time amid declining faith in multilateralism, heightened tension between big powers, the United States being seen as an unreliable partner in the face of China’s rise, and a spike in global conflicts.

A report in The Straits Times on November 18 said China was building a new runway on an island in Antelope Reef, which is part of the Paracel Islands in the South China Sea. The Paracel Islands are claimed by China, Vietnam, and Taiwan. The dispute is part of a broader Chinese claim to the whole of the South China Sea, where Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam have competing claims. Negotiations on a code of conduct in the South China Sea between China and ASEAN countries to prevent escalation of maritime friction have dragged on for two decades. This year’s summit, too, could not yield an agreement, though both China and ASEAN reported agreement on 80 percent of the draft.
It is against this backdrop that India’s proposals for deepening maritime engagement with ASEAN assume significance.
ASEAN has been a critical focus of India’s foreign policy since the 1990s, starting with the “Look East” policy, which was upgraded to the “Act East” policy in 2014.

With tensions in West Asia continuing unabated, India views ASEAN as key for economic growth, trade, and resources. India’s interest in the South China Sea stems from the fact that 55 percent of its trade to the region passes through the South China Sea and Malacca Straits. Consequently, India views ASEAN as a “locomotive for peace, stability and economic prosperity.”

India’s outreach to ASEAN also comes ahead of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit hosted by China on November 18-19, where leaders of China, the U.S. and Russia are expected to meet amid speculation that the three countries could take decisions with implications for other countries in the economic and security domains.

As Gurjit Singh, former Indian ambassador to Indonesia, observed, India-ASEAN cooperation benefits both as it gives them options beyond dealing with the big powers, amid the fragmentation in the world today. It is not surprising, therefore, that New Delhi views the grouping “as a consistent partner.”
